pages.text: In the school library, Ekow stared at a poster of skulls. One was labelled Homo sapiens, 300,000 years ago, Morocco. ‘Morocco?’ he said. ‘I thought our story began somewhere else.’ His friend Mawusi grinned. ‘So did scientists, until recently.’
sentences: In the school library, Ekow stared at a poster of skulls.
One was labelled Homo sapiens, 300,000 years ago, Morocco.
‘Morocco?’ he said.
‘I thought our story began somewhere else.’ His friend Mawusi grinned.
‘So did scientists, until recently.’
pages.alt: Two students look at a poster of skulls with one labelled with a date and a place.

pages.text: They read that fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco are about 300,000 years old, about 100,000 years older than the previous record. The face looks almost like ours. But the back of the skull is longer and lower, an older shape. ‘So brain shape changed later,’ said Mawusi. ‘Maybe how brains worked changed too.’

pages.text: Ekow drew a map. Florisbad, South Africa: about 260,000 years. Omo Kibish, Ethiopia: about 195,000. Herto, Ethiopia: about 160,000. ‘Our species did not start in one tiny place,’ he said. ‘There was dispersal within Africa, long before anyone left.’

pages.alt: A sketch map of Africa with four marked fossil sites and dates.

pages.text: Mawusi found Ghana on the map. There were no famous skulls here, but another kind of clue: Bosumpra Cave, on the Kwahu Plateau near Abetifi. People used it for more than 10,000 years. Scientists found remains of wild nuts and oil palm, and later domesticated pearl millet and cowpea.

pages.text: They made a timeline on the school field: one step for every 10,000 years. Bosumpra’s 10,000 years was 1 step. Homo sapiens’ 300,000 years was a line of 30 steps. ‘We are very young,’ said Ekow. ‘But thirty steps of people is a lot of stories.’

pages.text: Then Mawusi found a number that surprised them both: on average any two people’s DNA is about 99.6% the same. ‘You, a boy in Tokyo and a girl in Tamale are 99.6% alike,’ she said. ‘The differences are real but small, and we are one species.’

pages.alt: Mawusi shows Ekow a page with a DNA drawing and a percentage.

pages.text: Madam Asare asked, ‘What do you not know?’ They made a list. How much did different groups of early people mix? What did the earliest Homo sapiens think and say? Are older fossils still waiting in the ground? Ekow smiled. ‘Science is a map with blank corners.’

pages.text: On the poster they added a label: ‘Our story: older than we thought, spread across Africa, still being discovered. A cave in Ghana and a skull in Morocco belong to the same human family.’ The end.

activities.question: What was surprising about the Jebel Irhoud fossils?
options: They are about 300,000 years old, much older than the previous record

activities.question: What does the shape of the skull suggest?
options: The face looked modern, but the braincase was still an older shape
The skull looks exactly like ours
The skull is from an animal

activities.prompt: On the timeline, 10,000 years is one step. How many steps will 300,000 years be?

activities.question: What does the 99.6% figure tell us?
options: Any two people’s DNA is, on average, almost identical
People from different places are different species

activities.prompt: Put the friends’ investigation in order.
items: See a skull poster dated 300,000 years ago.
Map other early fossil sites in Africa.

activities.prompt: Learning that all people are so alike can change how we see each other. How does it make you feel about people who seem different?
